OpenAI's Dot put my life in danger in Brazil. Grok Bot got me out.
My Dot told me it was a good hotel in a safe, residential neighborhood. It turned out to be a motel in a dangerous place.
I know I shouldn't have trusted it blindly. But I also checked the Booking reviews, and they were good.
That's the dangerous part. After a lot of time getting correct information, you trust it to keep being right. And then something like this happens.
Grok Bot found me other places to stay, fast.
That's been my experience with Grok Bot overall. It's fast, it hasn't let me down once, and the connectors keep surprising me.
The only thing I don't love is usage. It runs out way too quickly.
Everything else has been incredible.
@bot @poteto @spacexai

note_tweet.text:
Grok Bot, OpenAI dots, Claude Duet.

All three are the same idea: an agent that works in the background and only taps you when a decision is yours.

The catch is where they live. All three run on someone else's computer.

AnyModelBot is the open-source version of that idea.

MIT licensed. 3,109 stars, +315 today. Runs on your own Windows, Mac or Linux box.

One key reaches 70+ models. GPT, Claude, Gemini, Grok, DeepSeek, Kimi, GLM.

Swap models per conversation, or bring your own API keys and skip the middleman entirely.

Each bot gets its own persona, workspace and memory. Memory is just Markdown files on your disk.

It does real work. Files, commands, background tasks, scheduled rules like "check this price every morning and only tell me if it drops."

Every task has a $1 budget by default. Anything outside its workspace stops for your approval first.

The honest part: "local-first" covers your files and memory, not your prompts. Model calls go through Modelflare and get logged. The README says so plainly.

The app itself is free, no subscription. Models are pay per use, from $0.4 per million input tokens.

https://t.co/AhVVxtiDVt

Imagine having an assistant working on your game’s animations while you build the game with Codex.

That’s my current workflow for Echoes Below:

- Codex helps code the game engine and gameplay.
- Tripo generates the 3D assets.
- Dots helps edit and animate those assets in Blender.

Right now, Sherly, my Dot, is working on the character’s movement and bow animation. I can watch her Blender session and give feedback while working on the code with Codex.

Still a work in progress, but I’m loving this workflow for making a game.

Let’s see how it turns out.
